fixes.explanation: Burnt offerings aren't mentioned in verse 2. The writer says the blessed “…seek Him with all their heart.” That's how the verse describes the seeking. I think that's worth chewing on for a minute.

Verse 3 says it straight: “They do no iniquity; they walk in His ways.” The writer is describing the blessed people he just mentioned. Notice the walking and the not doing iniquity are in the very same breath.

Nope, hiding isn't in the verse. In verse 5 he wishes his ways “…were committed to keeping Your statutes!” Then in verse 6 he says, “Then I would not be ashamed when I consider all Your commandments.” I think he wants to face those commandments.
Ha, winning arguments isn't in this verse, friend. The writer says he hid God's word in his heart “…that I might not sin against You.” That's the reason the text gives. Not a debate trophy in sight.

Verse 12 doesn't mention a sign. He says, “Blessed are You, O LORD; teach me Your statutes.” He's asking to be taught, not handed a signal. I think that's a student talking, not someone waiting on fireworks.

Verse 17 says, “Deal bountifully with Your servant, that I may live and keep Your word.” The text gives the purpose right there. He wants to live and keep God's word. I think it's like asking for plenty of dough so the batch actually gets baked.

Verse 18 says, “Open my eyes that I may see wondrous things from Your law.” That's a request, not a report. He's asking God to open his eyes to the wondrous things from the law. I think that's a humble way to come to the Word.
His enemies aren't in this verse. He prays, “Open my eyes that I may see wondrous things from Your law.” What he wants to see comes from God's law. I think that's a prayer worth borrowing.

Verse 19 doesn't ask about servants. It says, “do not hide Your commandments from me.” That's the thing he wants in the open. In verse 17 he calls himself God's servant, but verse 19 is about the commandments.

That's a very human guess, friend, and the text goes another way. Verse 23 says, “Though rulers sit and slander me, Your servant meditates on Your statutes.” The verse says he meditates, and slandering back isn't mentioned.

Verse 24 doesn't call God's testimonies enemies. It says, “Your testimonies are indeed my delight; they are my counselors.” To him they're on his side. Enemies show up elsewhere in this psalm (Psalm 119:98), but not here.
Secret isn't in verse 24. The writer says the testimonies are “my delight” and “my counselors.” Those are the two things he calls them, and secret isn't one of them.
